concepts.label: Mass in Physical and Chemical Changes
concepts.cardText: In Activity 9.1 the mass of a salt solution is equal to the sum of the masses of the water and salt taken, so there is practically no change in mass during the formation of a solution, which is a physical change; this is true for all physical changes. In Activity 9.2, vinegar and baking soda react to form carbon dioxide and other substances. In set-up 1, with the balloon not attached, brisk effervescence occurs and the final reading does not match the initial reading. In set-up 2, with the balloon fixed to the flask so the gas stays in, the final reading matches the initial reading. The total mass of vinegar and baking soda before the reaction equals the total mass of carbon dioxide and other substances formed after it, and in set-up 1 the difference occurs because the gas produced escapes.

concepts.label: The Law of Conservation of Mass
concepts.cardText: The activities show that the total mass remains the same before and after a chemical reaction, so matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. This is known as the Law of Conservation of Mass, proposed by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789; Lavoisier is known as the Father of Modern Chemistry and the law applies to every chemical reaction. In Activity 9.3 solutions of sodium sulfate and barium chloride are mixed in an open system, since no gas is formed, and a white precipitate of barium sulfate forms along with sodium chloride; the mass is unchanged. In Example 9.1, 4.0 g of calcium carbonate and 2.92 g of hydrochloric acid, a total of 6.92 g, give 1.76 g of carbon dioxide, 0.72 g of water and 4.44 g of calcium chloride, also 6.92 g, so the mass of reactants equals the mass of products and the law is obeyed.

concepts.label: The Law of Constant Proportions
concepts.cardText: Soon after Lavoisier, Joseph Proust proposed that in any compound formed by two or more elements, the elements combine in a fixed ratio by mass; in other words, elements in a compound have definite proportions irrespective of its source. Water collected from rivers, borewells or the ocean, once purified and analysed, always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8, so 9 g of purified water from any source gives 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen. This is known as the Law of Constant Proportions, the Law of Definite Proportions or Proust's Law. Over the centuries many civilisations found that heating cinnabar (hingula) yields mercury and sulfur in mass percentages of about 86.22% and 13.78%, and that grinding them together in this ratio forms cinnabar. In Example 9.3, sodium chloride contains sodium and chlorine in the mass ratio of 23:35.5.

concepts.label: Dalton's Postulates
concepts.cardText: The two laws discussed formed the basis of Dalton's Atomic Theory, which attempts to explain why substances combine in fixed proportions and why there is no loss or gain of mass in a chemical reaction. Dalton explained these by proposing that during a chemical reaction atoms are indivisible and merely rearrange, rather than being created or destroyed. A postulate is a fundamental assumption accepted as truth without formal proof from which further ideas are formed. Dalton postulated that all matter is made up of very tiny particles called atoms which participate in chemical reactions; atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction; atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties; atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties; atoms combine in the ratio of simple whole numbers to form compounds; and the relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound. For example, when magnesium burns in air a white powder of magnesium oxide forms, which shows that magnesium atoms have combined with oxygen atoms.

concepts.label: Molecules and Chemical Bonds
concepts.cardText: Atoms of an element can combine to form a molecule of that element, for example a hydrogen molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms, and atoms of different elements combine to form a molecule of a compound, for example one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom combine to form hydrogen chloride. A molecule is an electrically neutral entity consisting of more than one atom that is capable of independent existence and shows all the properties of that substance. Some elements such as helium exist only as atoms because their atoms are stable. Atoms with 8 electrons in the outermost shell (2 if the K shell is the outermost) are stable; if the valence shell has fewer than eight, atoms may share, gain or lose electrons to complete it, and in this process atoms of elements combine to form compounds. This generally takes place in two ways: sharing of electrons, and transfer of electrons. When atoms combine the total energy of the system becomes lower than the sum of the energies of the individual atoms, making the arrangement more stable. The force that holds atoms together is called a chemical bond.

concepts.label: Covalent Bond: Molecules of Elements
concepts.cardText: Hydrogen has only one electron in its K shell, and since the K shell can have two electrons it needs one more to become stable, so a hydrogen atom shares one electron with another hydrogen atom to form a hydrogen molecule, H2. The shared pair of electrons attracts both the nuclei and makes the molecule stable. This interaction between atoms through a shared pair of electrons is called a covalent bond; if two atoms are joined by sharing one electron each they are joined by a single bond, depicted as H-H. A chlorine atom has seven valence electrons and needs one electron, so two chlorine atoms share one electron each to form a chlorine molecule, Cl-Cl, joined by a single covalent bond. An oxygen atom has six valence electrons and needs two more to complete its octet, so two oxygen atoms share two electrons each to form an oxygen molecule, held together by two pairs of shared electrons in a double bond, O=O.

concepts.label: Covalent Compounds: Hydrogen Chloride and Water
concepts.cardText: When atoms of two different elements combine, as in hydrogen chloride, both hydrogen and chlorine need one electron each to attain a stable configuration (hydrogen to complete its duplet and chlorine its octet), so they share one electron each to form a molecule of hydrogen chloride. Since the hydrogen and chlorine atoms bond by sharing electrons, it is a covalent compound, and since they share one pair of electrons they are bonded by a single bond, H-Cl. Hydrogen needs one electron while oxygen needs two, so oxygen cannot simply share two with an atom that needs only one; this is achieved by two hydrogen atoms each sharing an electron with one oxygen atom, forming a water molecule, H2O, which indicates the presence of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Atoms can also release enormous energy when their nuclei split or combine, which is atomic or nuclear energy.

concepts.label: Naming Covalent Compounds
concepts.cardText: Covalent compounds are named by indicating the number of atoms of each element using a prefix system. The first element retains its regular name, while the second element ends in -ide. Prefixes such as mono- (1), di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4), penta- (5) and hexa- (6) indicate the number of atoms. Mono- is usually omitted for the first element but used for the second. If a prefix ends with o or a and the element starts with a vowel the last vowel is dropped, as in monoxide and pentoxide; if the prefix ends with i it is kept, as in dioxide and trioxide. CO is carbon monoxide, CO2 is carbon dioxide, CS2 is carbon disulfide, PCl3 is phosphorus trichloride, SF6 is sulfur hexafluoride, N2O4 is dinitrogen tetroxide and N2O5 is dinitrogen pentoxide. When hydrogen is the first element no prefix is added before it, so H2S is hydrogen sulfide. A few binary compounds are known only by common names: H2O is water and NH3 is ammonia.

concepts.label: Ionic Bond: Transfer of Electrons
concepts.cardText: If the valence shell of an atom has fewer than four electrons it generally donates its valence electrons to achieve a stable configuration, and atoms with more than four valence electrons usually gain or share electrons to complete an octet. Sodium (atomic number 11) has one valence electron and attains a stable configuration by losing it; it then has 11 protons and 10 electrons and becomes a positively charged sodium cation, Na+. A chlorine atom has seven valence electrons and attains a stable configuration by gaining one electron from another atom; after gaining it, it acquires a negative charge and is called a chloride anion, Cl-. Cations and anions are collectively called ions. Once formed, the sodium and chloride ions are held together by the electrostatic force of attraction due to their opposite charges, and this force of attraction between oppositely charged ions is called an ionic bond. Atoms such as sulfur gain two electrons to form S2-.

concepts.label: Crystal Structure of Ionic Compounds
concepts.cardText: Ionic compounds usually do not remain as single units; they form three-dimensional crystals in which ions are arranged in a repeating pattern. In sodium chloride each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions, and each chloride ion is surrounded by six sodium ions. These oppositely charged ions are arranged in a regular, repeating 3-D pattern known as a crystal structure. The crystal structure is represented as a crystal lattice, with ions depicted as points or dots, which helps to visualise the arrangement of ions in the crystal.

concepts.label: Naming Ionic Compounds and Polyatomic Ions
concepts.cardText: In naming ionic compounds, the name of the cation is written first, followed by the name of the anion. Names of simple anions end with -ide. Generally metals form cations and non-metals form anions, and ionic compounds are typically formed when metals combine with non-metals, for example sodium chloride, calcium oxide and magnesium sulfide. Some ions are formed by the combination of atoms of two or more elements and are called polyatomic ions; the names of polyatomic ions generally do not end with -ide.

concepts.label: Writing Formulae of Covalent Compounds
concepts.cardText: A chemical formula for a covalent compound can be written quickly in three steps: write the symbols of the constituent elements of the compound; write the valencies of these elements; and cross over the valencies of the combining atoms and write them as subscripts after the symbols. For hydrogen chloride, hydrogen and chlorine each have a valency of one, so the formula is HCl; if the valency is one after criss-crossing it is not written. For hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen has valency 1 and sulfur 2, so the formula is H2S. For carbon tetrachloride, carbon has valency 4 and chlorine 1, so the formula is CCl4.

concepts.label: Writing Formulae of Ionic Compounds
concepts.cardText: To write the formula of an ionic compound, write the symbol of the cation first, followed by the symbol of the anion; write the charges under the symbols rather than as superscripts; and cross over the charges, only the numbers, to obtain the formula. The chemical formula gives the simplest ratio of the elements in a compound, so after criss-crossing the subscripts are divided by a common factor, if any. In calcium chloride (Ca2+ and Cl-) the formula is CaCl2, with two chloride ions for each calcium ion, so the positive and negative charges balance and the overall structure is neutral. In aluminium oxide (Al3+ and O2-) the formula is Al2O3. For magnesium oxide, criss-crossing gives Mg2O2, which is simply written as MgO. The same method works for polyatomic ions: magnesium hydroxide is Mg(OH)2 and calcium carbonate is CaCO3. Brackets are used when two or more polyatomic ions of the same type are present, as in Al(OH)3, and not required when only one polyatomic anion is present. The charges on the ions are not indicated in the formula.

concepts.topicTitle: Properties of compounds and their masses
concepts.label: Properties of Ionic and Covalent Compounds
concepts.cardText: Ionic compounds such as sodium chloride and copper sulfate are generally soluble in water but insoluble in solvents such as kerosene and petrol. In contrast, most covalent compounds, such as camphor and naphthalene, are insoluble in water but dissolve in kerosene and petrol. Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in the solid state because their ions are held in fixed positions by strong forces; to conduct, ions must be free to move, which occurs only when ionic compounds are dissolved in water. Some covalent compounds, such as sugar, are soluble in water but do not provide ions in solution and so do not conduct electricity, and other covalent compounds such as camphor and naphthalene also do not conduct electricity. Ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points due to strong inter-ionic attractions, whereas covalent compounds usually have low melting and boiling points.

concepts.topicTitle: Properties of compounds and their masses
concepts.label: Molecular Mass and Formula Unit Mass
concepts.cardText: Since the formulae of covalent compounds are known, the mass of a molecule is found by adding up the masses of the atoms present in it; this is the molecular mass. For water, with H = 1 u and O = 16 u, the molecular mass is (1 u times 2) plus (16 u times 1) which is 18 u, and for carbon dioxide with C = 12 u it is 12 + 32 = 44 u. In ionic compounds the ions form 3-D crystals, so ionic compounds do not form molecules. Instead, the collection of the simplest whole number ratio of ions is termed a formula unit, and the mass of a formula unit is called the formula unit mass. For sodium oxide, Na2O, with Na = 23 u and O = 16 u, the formula unit mass is 62 u, and for calcium nitrate, Ca(NO3)2, it is 164 u.
